extra.message: Flask Debug Mode Enabled Exposing Interactive Console — Remote code execution via the Werkzeug debugger's interactive console if an attacker triggers an unhandled exception, plus full source code and variable disclosure via stack traces. [verified: Same as finding [0]: app.run(host='0.0.0.0', debug=True, port=5000) exposes the Werkzeug debugger console on a reachable network port, enabling RCE on unhandled exceptions.]

Flask Debug Mode Enabled in Production — The Werkzeug debugger console can be accessed if the PIN is guessed (potentially predictable in container environments). Full source code, secrets, and environment variables are leaked in tracebacks. Enables arbitrary code execution via the debugger console. [verified: app.run(host='0.0.0.0', debug=True, port=5000) at line 228 enables the Werkzeug interactive debugger on a network-exposed port mapped via docker-compose; triggering any unhandled exception grants arbitrary Python code execution.]

Hardcoded JWT Signing Secret — Attacker can forge JWT tokens to impersonate any user, bypassing all token-based authentication and gaining access to any account. [verified: Identical root cause to findings [0] and [1]: the hardcoded string 'secret' is used for both JWT signing (auth_routes.py:48) and verification (auth.py:23), enabling complete authentication bypass via token forgery.]

Hardcoded Weak JWT Secret Enabling Token Forgery — Complete authentication bypass—an attacker can forge valid JWT tokens for any user (including admins) and access all authenticated endpoints as any identity. [verified: Same hardcoded 'secret' string as finding [0] — used in jwt.encode at auth_routes.py:48 and jwt.decode at auth.py:23. An attacker can trivially guess this secret and forge tokens for arbitrary user IDs.]

SQL Injection in User Registration — Attacker can insert arbitrary data into the database, modify other users' records, or extract sensitive information via subqueries or time-based techniques. [verified: Attacker-supplied username from POST /api/register is interpolated directly into a raw f-string SQL INSERT with no parameterization, sanitization, or middleware; the ORM duplicate check on line 19 does not sanitize the value before it hits line 22.]

SQL Injection in Login — Attacker can extract password hashes, user PII (SSN, DOB, balances), and all database contents via UNION or blind SQL injection. [verified: Attacker-supplied username from POST /api/login is interpolated directly into a raw f-string SELECT query with no parameterization or input sanitization whatsoever.]

IDOR - Update Any User's Password (Account Takeover) — Any authenticated attacker can change the password of any other user (including seed users with high balances), taking over their account and funds. [verified: Same IDOR as findings [3] and [9]; update_password lacks any check that the supplied user_id matches current_user.id, enabling arbitrary password changes and account takeover.]

IDOR - Arbitrary Password Change for Any User — Full account takeover—an attacker can reset any user's password and then log in as that user, gaining access to their balance, profile (SSN, DOB), and transactions. [verified: Same IDOR as finding [3]; update_password accepts arbitrary user_id from the request body with no ownership check against current_user.id, permitting full account takeover.]

IDOR - Arbitrary Password Reset for Any User — Complete account takeover of any user. An attacker can change an admin or high-balance user's password and log in as them. [verified: POST /api/update-password accepts user_id from the request body and updates that user's password with zero check against current_user.id; any authenticated user can take over any account.]

Insecure YAML Deserialization leading to Remote Code Execution — Attacker can achieve arbitrary code execution on the backend server, gaining full control over the application and underlying host. [verified: Same YAML deserialization RCE as findings [2] and [8]; yaml.load with unsafe Loader on attacker-controlled input permits arbitrary code execution.]

SQL Injection and IDOR in Transaction Listing — Authenticated attacker can view any user's transactions and execute arbitrary SQL via the `user_id` parameter to exfiltrate entire database contents. [verified: Duplicate of findings 0/2/6: user_id from request.args at line 41 is directly interpolated into raw SQL at line ~43 with no parameterization and no ownership verification; the @token_required decorator does not neutralize either vulnerability.]

SQL Injection in Transaction Search — Authenticated attacker can execute arbitrary SQL queries to read, modify, or delete any data in the database including user credentials and financial records. [verified: Duplicate of findings 1/5: the description query parameter from line 71 is interpolated into a LIKE clause at line ~75 via f-string without parameterization; no intervening sanitization or escaping exists.]

SQL Injection in Transaction Search — Attacker can extract all database contents via UNION injection, including password hashes, PII, and transaction history for all users. [verified: The description search_term from request.args.get('description', '') at line 78 is concatenated into a LIKE clause via f-string at line ~80 with no parameterization; no WAF, middleware, or sanitization intervenes.]

Permissive CORS - Origin Reflection with Credentials — A malicious website can make authenticated API requests on behalf of a victim if the attacker obtains the JWT token (e.g., via localStorage access from any XSS on the same origin, or social engineering). [verified: The after_request handler at lines 50-58 reflects any Origin header into Access-Control-Allow-Origin with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials:true, allowing any malicious origin to make credentialed cross-origin requests using the JWT Bearer token.]

Permissive CORS with Credentials - Any Origin Allowed — Malicious websites can make authenticated API requests on behalf of victims, enabling full account takeover through CSRF-style attacks that bypass same-origin policy. [verified: Same as finding [1]: the CORS after_request handler at lines 54-59 mirrors the Origin header into Access-Control-Allow-Origin alongside Access-Control-Allow-Credentials:true, fully permissive cross-origin access.]

Weak Password Hashing - MD5 Without Salt — If the database is compromised, all user passwords can be cracked in seconds using rainbow tables or GPU-accelerated brute force. [verified: Same unsalted MD5 hash in models.py set_password/check_password, reachable via POST /api/register and /api/login; no salt, no key-stretching, enabling instant rainbow-table recovery of all passwords from the database.]

Weak Password Hashing with Unsalted MD5 — Attacker with database access can trivially crack all user passwords using rainbow tables or brute-force at billions of hashes per second on commodity hardware. [verified: Identical unsalted-MD5 hashing in models.py line 23 area (set_password body); identical passwords produce identical hashes, and no compensating bcrypt/PBKDF2/salt exists — full password compromise if the SQLite DB is exposed.]

Weak Password Hashing - Unsalted MD5 — All user passwords are crackable with commodity hardware in minutes. An attacker with database access can recover every plaintext password. [verified: set_password at models.py:24 uses hashlib.md5(password.encode()).hexdigest() with no salt and no iteration count; MD5 is trivially crackable via rainbow tables and GPU brute-force, and the hash is reachable on registration/login.]

Missing Rate Limiting and Brute-Force Protection on Authentication Endpoints — Attacker can perform unlimited brute-force password guessing and user enumeration against login and registration endpoints without any throttling or lockout. [verified: Same missing rate limiting as finding [4] spanning both /api/login and /api/register; no Flask-Limiter, lockout, or CAPTCHA present anywhere, enabling unlimited brute-force and enumeration.]

Missing Rate Limiting on Login - Brute Force — Attacker can brute-force passwords via automated dictionary attacks. Combined with known usernames (from enumeration) and MD5 hashing, account compromise is fast and reliable. [verified: No rate limiting, account lockout, CAPTCHA, or progressive delay exists on /api/login or anywhere in the app; combined with MD5 password hashing this enables fast automated brute-force.]

Negative Amount Transfer Allows Fund Theft — Authenticated attacker can steal funds from any user by specifying a negative transfer amount, resulting in direct financial loss for the victim and unauthorized enrichment of the attacker. [verified: Duplicate of finding 4: amount at line 14 is parsed without positivity check, allowing negative values to bypass the balance check at line 30 and steal funds via the arithmetic at lines 33-34.]

Negative Amount Transfer Allows Theft from Other Users — Attacker can steal money from any other user by sending a negative transfer amount, gaining funds while the victim loses them [verified: amount at line 16 is parsed as Decimal(str(data.get('amount',0))) with no positivity validation; a negative amount bypasses the balance check (5000 < -100 is False), and the arithmetic at lines 33-34 steals from the receiver while crediting the attacker.]

Negative Amount Transfer Enables Theft From Other Users — Authenticated attacker can steal arbitrary funds from any other user by sending negative transfer amounts, effectively draining victim accounts [verified: Duplicate of findings 4/7: amount at line 16 lacks a positivity guard; negative amounts circumvent the balance check and reverse the transfer direction, enabling theft from any target user.]

Race Condition / TOCTOU in Money Transfer — Attacker can overdraw their account by sending concurrent transfer requests that all pass the balance check before any debit is committed, effectively creating money or stealing funds. [verified: The balance check at line 30 and the debit/credit at lines 33-34 are not atomic; with isolation_level=None (autocommit) and no SELECT FOR UPDATE or explicit row lock, concurrent requests can both pass the balance check before either commits, enabling overdraft.]

IDOR - View Any User's Transaction History — Attacker can enumerate all user transaction histories including amounts, counterparties, and descriptions, violating financial privacy across all accounts. [verified: Duplicate of finding 2: user_id from request.args at line 41 is used directly with no ownership check against current_user.id, allowing any authenticated user to view another user's full transaction history.]

IDOR - View Any User's Transactions — Attacker can enumerate all users' financial transaction histories, revealing who transacted with whom, amounts, and descriptions across the entire bank. [verified: The user_id query parameter at line 47 defaults to current_user.id but accepts any caller-supplied value with no ownership check (e.g., if int(user_id) != current_user.id), allowing any authenticated user to enumerate other users' transaction histories.]

Missing Security Headers (CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options) — Application is vulnerable to clickjacking, MIME-type confusion attacks, and lacks browser-enforced content security policies [verified: No CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options, or X-Content-Type-Options headers are set anywhere in the after_request handler or elsewhere; the app is vulnerable to clickjacking and MIME-sniffing attacks.]

Verbose Error Messages Leaking Internal Application Details — Attacker gains detailed stack traces, file paths, and internal code structure, significantly aiding reconnaissance for targeted exploits. [verified: The 404 handler (line 65) and 500 handler (line 70) both return str(error) to the client; combined with debug=True, detailed tracebacks, file paths, and local variables are exposed to attackers.]

Cleartext HTTP — No TLS/HTTPS for Credentials and Sensitive Data — An attacker on the same network can sniff cleartext credentials, JWT tokens, PII including SSNs, and financial transaction data [verified: app.run() has no ssl_context, docker-compose exposes plain HTTP ports only, and no TLS termination is configured anywhere; credentials, JWT tokens, and PII traverse the network in cleartext.]

Username Enumeration via Registration Error Message — An attacker can build a list of valid usernames for targeted password attacks, social engineering, or account takeover via the IDOR password-reset vulnerability. [verified: Same user enumeration as finding [5]; distinct 'Username already exists' error on registration allows attackers to build a list of valid usernames with no countermeasure.]

No Server-Side Token Invalidation on Logout — Stolen JWT tokens remain usable after user logout for up to 24 hours; no way for users to revoke compromised sessions [verified: POST /api/logout is a no-op returning only a JSON message; there is no server-side token blocklist or revocation mechanism, so stolen JWTs remain valid up to 24 hours after logout.]

JWT Token Stored in Browser localStorage (XSS-Prone) — Any XSS vulnerability on the page can instantly steal the JWT token, enabling session hijacking and full account takeover. [verified: JWT token is stored in localStorage (App.js:52) and read at multiple call sites (App.js:18,28,68) with no HttpOnly cookie fallback; no CSP, X-Frame-Options, or other XSS-mitigation headers exist anywhere in the backend, so any XSS on the origin can trivially steal the token for full account takeover — but exploitation requires a separate XSS vector, making this medium severity.]

Hardcoded Flask SECRET_KEY in Source Code and Docker Compose — Flask session cookies can be forged if session-based features are ever used. The key is exposed in git history and Docker environment. [verified: SECRET_KEY='supersecret' is hardcoded at line 16 and in docker-compose.yml; Flask sessions are not currently used (JWT with separate secret handles auth), but the hardcoded key remains in source control as an anti-pattern.]

Hardcoded Flask SECRET_KEY — Attacker can forge Flask session cookies if session-based features are used, and the weak key undermines all Flask cryptographic operations relying on SECRET_KEY. [verified: Same as finding [6]: hardcoded SECRET_KEY='supersecret' at line 16; impact is low because the app authenticates via JWT with a separate 'secret' key rather than Flask sessions.]
